idiom_name: JPA EntityManager with FlushModeType.COMMIT / Hibernate session
implementation_notes: The persistence context is the write-behind buffer: entity state changes are tracked in memory and Hibernate's Session - in its own documentation - monitors changes and executes SQL in a write-behind fashion. JPA exposes the deferral through FlushModeType.COMMIT, whose contract is that flushing occurs at transaction commit, so a service that sets COMMIT (or relies on the default commit-time flush) coalesces repeated modifications of the same entity into one UPDATE. Call EntityManager#flush when a query must observe pending state; what replaces the classic structure is the container-managed persistence context, with no dirty map or flusher of your own.
pitfalls: With FlushModeType.COMMIT the effect of updates on queries is unspecified: a JPQL query can miss the change you just made unless you flush first.
The persistence context is not thread-safe and must not outlive its transaction; detached entities silently drop staged changes.
Optimistic-lock failures surface as OptimisticLockException at commit, far from the code that staged the change.

variants.name: Infinispan write-behind cache store
variants.idiom_name: Infinispan cache store with the <write-behind> element
variants.implementation_notes: For cache-fronted workloads the deferral moves into the data grid: an Infinispan cache store configured with the write-behind element acknowledges the cache write and queues the modification, flushing to the backing store asynchronously with configurable modification-queue size, thread pool and failure behaviour. Unlike the ORM flush this buffer is shared and survives the request, so durability depends on the grid's queue and its failure policy rather than on the database transaction.
variants.code_sketch:
<!-- clustered-cache or local-cache configuration -->
<distributed-cache name="people">
  <persistence passivation="false">
    <jdbc:string-keyed-jdbc-store fetch-state="false">
      <write-behind modification-queue-size="1024"
                    fail-silent="false"
                    thread-pool-size="2"/>
    </jdbc:string-keyed-jdbc-store>
  </persistence>
</distributed-cache>
pitfalls: fail-silent write-behind drops store failures by default: choose fail-silent=false or monitor the queue when loss is unacceptable.
The modification queue is bounded - on overflow, entries are coalesced or dropped according to configuration, so size it against the write rate.
A cache-store flush is not transactional with the cache write: a crash can lose queued changes even though the cache acknowledged them.
